sourceCheck: Checked on 2026-10-03. Release pins: Linux man-pages 6.19; GNU coreutils 9.12; Bash 5.3; GNU grep 3.12; GNU sed 4.10; GNU findutils 4.11.0; GNU gawk 5.4.1; GNU tar 1.35; systemd 262; OpenSSH 10.5/10.5p1; stable Linux kernel 7.2.8. The stable kernel is the release marked stable at https://www.kernel.org/, not the mainline release candidate. Version sources opened: https://www.kernel.org/doc/man-pages/; https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal.7.html including its COLOPHON; https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/coreutils/; https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/bash/; https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/grep/; https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/sed/; https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/findutils/; https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/gawk/; https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/tar/; the coreutils 9.12 release announcement containing NEWS at https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/coreutils-announce/2026-09/msg00000.html; https://github.com/systemd/systemd/releases/tag/v262; and https://www.openssh.com/releasenotes.html. Access limitations: the requested GNU full HTML manuals did not return usable content, so the permitted GNU release-listing and man7 fallbacks were used. The findutils 4.11.0 NEWS file was not independently retrieved; its release listing and find(1)'s FUNCTIONAL CHANGES were available. The freedesktop.org latest systemd pages returned 403, so their official v262 XML sources were read instead. Fedora's DNF quick-docs page returned a bot challenge; the Fedora change proposal and DNF5 documentation were available. These failed fetches are not counted as verified manual content. Man7 pages opened and COLOPHON provenance checked, using https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/manN/NAME.N.html: hier(7), path_resolution(7), inode(7), link(2), rename(2), symlink(2), symlink(7), ln(1), mount(8), df(1), du(1), mv(1), rm(1), readlink(1), chmod(1), chmod(2), chown(2), chgrp(1), unlink(2), ls(1), umask(2), execve(2), credentials(7), capabilities(7), passwd(5), shadow(5), sudo(8), sudoers(5), su(1), newgrp(1), usermod(8), ps(1), wait(2), prctl(2), PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER(2const), pidfd_open(2), signal(7), kill(1), nohup(1), environ(7), bash(1), grep(1), sed(1), gawk(1), find(1), xargs(1), sort(1), uniq(1), cut(1), tail(1), tar(1), ssh-copy-id(1), dpkg(1), and rpm(8). The kernel and C-library pages are from man-pages 6.19. The checked coreutils command pages are from coreutils 9.11, not 9.12; sed(1) is from sed 4.10. The shadow, newgrp and usermod pages are from shadow-utils 4.19.0. The ssh-copy-id page is from OpenSSH 9.9p2. Bash, grep, find, xargs, gawk, tar, ps, kill, mount, su, sudo, sudoers, dpkg and rpm pages identify upstream Git snapshots rather than release tarballs. Such snapshots are used for established behavior, not as evidence that a new feature shipped in the pinned release. Other section sources opened: https://uapi-group.org/specifications/specs/linux_file_system_hierarchy/; https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/FHS_3.0/fhs/index.html and its ch03s06, ch03s07, ch03s14, ch03s17, ch04, ch05 and ch05s15 pages; https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/sysctl/fs.html; https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/v262/sysctl.d/50-default.conf; https://man.openbsd.org/ssh; https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config; https://man.openbsd.org/scp; https://man.openbsd.org/ssh-keygen; https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/apt/apt.8.en.html; https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/apt/apt-get.8.en.html; https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Changes/SwitchToDnf5; https://dnf5.readthedocs.io/en/latest/; and https://dnf5.readthedocs.io/en/latest/dnf5.conf.5.html. The OpenBSD manuals track OpenBSD-current, so version-sensitive OpenSSH facts are checked against the release notes. Systemd content was read from the official repository, using its raw-file view: man/systemctl.xml, man/systemd.unit.xml, man/systemd.service.xml, man/systemd.kill.xml, man/systemd.special.xml, man/journalctl.xml and man/journald.conf.xml under https://github.com/systemd/systemd/tree/v262/man; https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/NEWS; and NEWS at tags v255, v258, v259, v260 and v262. NEWS confirms removal of split/unmerged-/usr support in 255, cgroup v1 and the legacy runlevel-control interfaces in 258, and System V service scripts, their generator and rc-local support in 260. Runlevel targets are available through an optional compatibility build setting in 260, not as an unconditional current interface. Since 259, upstream journal storage defaults to persistent, but that default is build-time configurable. Scope corrections and qualifications: hier(7)'s historical separate-/usr wording is not used to describe merged-usr systems. Classical directory roles use FHS 3.0; /run and merged-/usr compatibility links use UAPI.9 version 0.1, which labels itself work in progress. No universal /tmp cleanup, tmpfs, merged-sbin or distribution-default claim is planned. The kernel sysctl documentation does not establish a universal protected_hardlinks or protected_symlinks default; systemd's v262 configuration sets both to 1, subject to overrides, and the card explicitly supplies its condition. In r11, a blanket claim that repository metadata is signed and checked is unsupported across the named managers: DNF5 documents repo_gpgcheck as false by default, distinct from package-signature checking. That universal claim is excluded. OpenSSH release notes confirm the scp SFTP default since 9.0, Ed25519 key-generation default since 9.5, and DSA removal in 10.0; only the first is selected for a version-qualified card. Fedora's change page supports the Fedora 41-and-later DNF5 scope. find(1) documents the changed -mount behavior in 4.11.0, so -mount is excluded. Recent cut character/whitespace behavior, Bash's newer command-substitution syntax, globskipdots and obsolete systemd interfaces are excluded. Permission questions concern ordinary Linux discretionary permission checks and successful operations where applicable, rather than unstated ACLs, immutable flags, read-only mounts or privilege overrides. Beyond these qualifications, no section needs replacement.

cards.statement: Mounting a filesystem over a populated directory hides that directory's existing entries.
cards.explanation: A mount covers the previous directory contents rather than erasing them. Unmounting reveals those contents again.

cards.statement: FHS places host-specific system configuration under `/etc`.
cards.explanation: FHS reserves /etc for configuration specific to the host, rather than installed program binaries.

cards.statement: On merged-usr systems, `/bin` holds separate copies of the executables in `/usr/bin`.
cards.explanation: On merged-usr systems, /bin is a compatibility symlink to /usr/bin, so both paths reach the same installed executables.
cards.misconception: The compatibility directory duplicates executable files.

source.title: UAPI.9 Linux File System Hierarchy — version 0.1

cards.statement: FHS uses `/usr` as the standard parent directory for users' personal home directories.
cards.explanation: FHS assigns /usr to shareable installed resources, including commands, libraries and documentation, rather than personal home directories.
cards.misconception: The name /usr means that it contains user home directories.

cards.statement: FHS places changing system data, such as print spool contents, under `/var`.
cards.explanation: FHS uses /var for variable data, including spools, logs and administrative state that changes during operation.

cards.statement: FHS treats `/var/tmp` contents as temporary data to clear during system boot.
cards.explanation: FHS intends /var/tmp files to survive reboots. A site may still remove older files under its cleanup policy.
cards.misconception: Temporary files in /var/tmp are intended to be discarded at boot.

source.title: FHS 3.0 — /var/tmp: Temporary files preserved between system reboots

cards.statement: Services use `/run` for current-boot runtime data, including local socket files.
cards.explanation: UAPI.9 describes /run as storage for runtime data and sockets that is cleared at boot, rather than retained service data.

source.title: UAPI.9 Linux File System Hierarchy — version 0.1

cards.statement: FHS assigns `/` as the recommended home directory for the root account.
cards.explanation: FHS recommends /root for the root account's home. It also permits the home location to be chosen by developers or local policy.
cards.misconception: The filesystem root is also the recommended home of the root account.

source.title: FHS 3.0 — /root: Home directory for the root user

cards.statement: Linux programs access devices through special files under `/dev`.
cards.explanation: The /dev directory contains device files that programs use as interfaces to devices, rather than ordinary stored documents.

cards.statement: The kernel stores `/proc` process information as ordinary disk-backed files.
cards.explanation: Linux exposes process and system information through the virtual proc filesystem. Its entries are kernel interfaces rather than ordinary disk files.
cards.misconception: Process information under /proc is stored as conventional files on disk.

cards.statement: FHS places site-specific data served by the host, such as website content, under `/srv`.
cards.explanation: FHS assigns /srv to data supplied by services at this site. It leaves the directory's internal organization to local needs.

source.title: FHS 3.0 — /srv: Data for services provided by this system

cards.statement: `df project/` totals the space consumed by files below the project directory.
cards.explanation: With a directory operand, df reports space usage for the filesystem containing that directory, rather than summing its subtree.
cards.misconception: A directory argument makes df calculate that directory tree's size.

cards.statement: For `cat logs/app.log`, Linux starts pathname lookup in cat's current working directory.
cards.explanation: A relative pathname starts from the calling process's working directory. Here, logs is looked up below that directory.

cards.statement: Bash expands an unquoted `~/notes` using HOME when that variable is set.
cards.explanation: Bash substitutes HOME for a leading unquoted ~. If HOME is unset, it uses the executing user's home directory.

cards.statement: Writing to a file through one hard link changes the contents read through its other hard links.
cards.explanation: Hard links name the same inode and data. A write updates the shared file rather than an independent copy.

cards.statement: GNU ln can place a hard link on a different mounted filesystem from its target.
cards.explanation: Linux requires a hard link and its target to belong to the same mounted filesystem. A cross-filesystem link attempt fails.
cards.misconception: Hard links can connect files across mounted filesystems.

cards.statement: Linux rejects an attempt to hard-link a directory even when the caller is root.
cards.explanation: Linux forbids directory hard links through link(). Administrative privilege does not provide an exception to that restriction.

cards.statement: GNU `ln -s` validates the target's existence before creating the new link.
cards.explanation: GNU ln -s accepts a target name that does not exist. The resulting symbolic link remains dangling until that name resolves.
cards.misconception: Creating a symbolic link requires an existing target.

cards.statement: Linux resolves a relative symlink target from the working directory where the link was created.
cards.explanation: A relative symbolic-link target starts from the directory containing the link. The link creation command's working directory is not recorded.
cards.misconception: Relative symlink targets retain the working directory used at creation.

cards.statement: `ln source alias` creates source as a new hard link to the existing file alias.
cards.explanation: In this two-operand form, ln takes the existing target first and the new link name second; alias is the new name.
cards.misconception: The first ln operand is the new link and the second is its existing target.

cards.statement: GNU readlink can print a symbolic link's stored target text using `readlink link`.
cards.explanation: In its basic form, GNU readlink prints the value stored in the symbolic link, retaining a relative target as relative text.

cards.statement: `rm link` follows a symbolic link named link and removes the file it points to.
cards.explanation: For a symbolic-link operand such as link, rm removes the link itself. The referenced file remains in place.
cards.misconception: Removing a symbolic link with rm removes its referent.

cards.statement: A same-filesystem rename can leave an open file descriptor referring to the renamed file.
cards.explanation: Linux rename() changes a file's pathname while existing open file descriptors keep referring to that file.

cards.statement: With fs.protected_hardlinks=1, read access alone lets an unprivileged user hard-link another user's file.
cards.explanation: With protected_hardlinks enabled, ownership or read-and-write access is needed. Read access alone does not satisfy the nonowner access check.
cards.misconception: Read access alone satisfies protected_hardlinks for an unprivileged nonowner.

source.title: Linux kernel documentation — File system sysctls

cards.statement: Linux can combine owner and matching group mode bits when checking the file owner's permissions.
cards.explanation: Linux selects the owner permission class for a file's owner. It does not add permissions from the group class.
cards.misconception: Owner and group permission bits combine when the owner belongs to the file's group.

cards.statement: A directory's read bit grants permission to traverse that directory during pathname lookup.
cards.explanation: Directory execute permission authorizes pathname searches through it. Directory read permission instead permits listing the names it contains.
cards.misconception: Directory read permission also provides search permission.

cards.statement: A file's write bit grants its owner permission to remove its name from the parent directory.
cards.explanation: Removing a file name needs write and search permission on the containing directory. The file's own write bit does not authorize that directory change.
cards.misconception: Write permission on a file authorizes deleting its directory entry.

cards.statement: `chmod g+w report` adds group write permission while retaining report's existing read bits.
cards.explanation: In a symbolic chmod mode, + adds the named permission. Using g+w leaves the file's existing read permissions intact.

cards.statement: `chmod 640 report` grants read permission to users who match the file's group class.
cards.explanation: The middle octal digit specifies the group permissions. A value of 4 supplies the group read bit.

cards.statement: GNU chmod's `a+X` grants execute permission on regular files that already have an execute bit.
cards.explanation: For a regular file, GNU chmod applies X when some execute bit is already set. This condition avoids making ordinary data files executable.

cards.statement: For a requested mode of 0666, `umask 000` can add execute permission to a new regular file.
cards.explanation: A umask removes requested permission bits; it does not introduce new ones. A requested mode of 0666 supplies no execute bits to preserve.
cards.misconception: A zero umask adds execute bits to the usual regular-file creation mode.

cards.statement: A file owner can give that file to another user with chown using ordinary owner permissions.
cards.explanation: Linux reserves ownership transfers for appropriately privileged processes. Mere file ownership does not grant that authority.
cards.misconception: File ownership includes the right to transfer ownership to another user.

cards.statement: A file's owner can use chgrp to select a group they belong to.
cards.explanation: Linux permits a file's owner to change its group to one of the owner's groups. This operation uses the existing membership.

cards.statement: `chmod 600 link` changes a Linux symbolic link's own mode bits.
cards.explanation: GNU chmod leaves symbolic-link permissions alone. For a symlink explicitly named on its command line, it changes the target's permissions.
cards.misconception: chmod changes the symbolic link's own permissions rather than the target's.

cards.statement: Bash can run a readable script via `bash script.sh` even when the script's execute bits are clear.
cards.explanation: With bash script.sh, Bash opens the script as input and executes the commands it reads. The script itself need not have execute permission.

cards.statement: On Linux, a file's owner can change its mode with chmod even when its write bit is clear.
cards.explanation: The file owner has authority to change permission bits. Changing file permissions and writing file contents are separate operations.

cards.statement: A setuid ELF executable can run with an effective UID different from the caller's real UID.
cards.explanation: When the set-user-ID bit takes effect, Linux sets the effective UID to the executable's owner while retaining the caller's real UID.

cards.statement: On Linux, a Bash script's setuid bit can grant the script owner's effective UID during direct execution.
cards.explanation: Linux ignores the set-user-ID bit on interpreter scripts. Setting that bit on a Bash script does not provide its owner's effective UID.
cards.misconception: The setuid bit on a directly executed interpreter script changes its effective UID.

cards.statement: Linux can honor an ELF file's setuid bit when executing it from a nosuid mount.
cards.explanation: On a nosuid mount, set-user-ID bits confer no privilege. Linux may ignore the bits or refuse execution, depending on kernel behavior.
cards.misconception: A nosuid mount still permits setuid privilege changes for binary executables.

cards.statement: A new file automatically inherits the group of a setgid parent directory.
cards.explanation: Linux uses a setgid directory's group for files created inside it, rather than the creating process's effective group.

cards.statement: A directory's sticky bit restricts who reads file contents inside that directory.
cards.explanation: The sticky bit adds deletion and renaming restrictions based on file ownership, directory ownership or privilege. It does not govern reading file contents.
cards.misconception: The sticky bit protects file content confidentiality instead of directory-entry removal.

cards.statement: On Linux, changing an executable file's owner clears that file's set-user-ID bit.
cards.explanation: Linux clears set-user-ID when an executable changes ownership, including changes performed by root. The earlier permission setting does not persist.

cards.statement: Linux capabilities can give a process selected privileges while its effective UID stays greater than zero.
cards.explanation: Capabilities separate privileged operations into individual permissions. A process can hold particular capabilities rather than acquiring full root privilege.

cards.statement: With default sudoers policy, sudo asks for the target user's password when authentication is needed.
cards.explanation: By default, sudoers authenticates the invoking user rather than the target account. Policy options can change whose password is requested.
cards.misconception: sudo normally authenticates using the target account's password.

cards.statement: With util-linux su, `su - alice` starts the login shell in alice's home directory.
cards.explanation: The login option makes util-linux su change to the target user's home directory before starting the login shell.

cards.statement: `/etc/passwd` stores the password hashes for local accounts that use shadow passwords.
cards.explanation: For local shadow-password accounts, hashes reside in /etc/shadow. The corresponding /etc/passwd field normally contains x instead.
cards.misconception: Shadow-password hashes are stored in the public passwd database.

cards.statement: `usermod -aG developers alice` retains alice's existing supplementary group memberships.
cards.explanation: The -a option appends the named groups to the current supplementary membership list. With -G alone, omitted memberships are removed.

cards.statement: Editing `/etc/group` automatically refreshes supplementary groups in existing login shells.
cards.explanation: Supplementary groups belong to process credentials. Editing the group database does not replace an existing shell's group list.
cards.misconception: A change in the group database immediately updates running processes' credentials.
